source.title: Can neural networks model the human perception of geometric shapes?
source.authors: Maxence Pajot; Théo Morfoisse; Mathias Sablé-Meyer; Yair Lakretz; S. Dehaene

record.tranche_reason: The study discusses the Platonic Representation Hypothesis, but its experiments measure alignment between vision models and human behavior, not convergence between independently trained models or the other behaviors specified by the claim versions.
record.gate_note: The study tests model-to-human alignment on geometric-shape tasks, including dataset-size trends and alternative distance metrics. Those results do not directly measure any claim version's named model-to-model, cross-modal, seed, mapping, or feature convergence. Reported results from cited studies are not included.
record.test_reason: The study measures how well vision models' representations align with human behavioural data on geometric-shape tasks, and how that alignment varies with dataset size, architecture, parameters and training method. It never compares representations between models, across seeds or across modalities on paired data, and does no mapping or feature matching. The Platonic Representation Hypothesis is invoked only in the Discussion, to interpret model-to-human results. The cross-task rank-order correlations (r12) correlate model rankings, not model representations.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely right. The authors conclude that scaling training data is the main driver of vision networks approximating human geometric-shape representations, ahead of architecture and parameter count. Networks beat the symbolic model in Exps 1–2 but fall short in Exp 3, where training method was the top predictor. The symbolic MDL still adds information in Exp 2. Alignment appeared to saturate in Exp 1 but not in Exps 2–3. They interpret model-to-human convergence as consistent with the Platonic Representation Hypothesis without measuring model-to-model similarity.
record.recipe_differences: The study does not apply the original Platonic Representation Hypothesis measurement; it measures vision-model alignment with human behavioral results on geometric-shape tasks.
record.method_sensitivity: For model-to-human alignment, results are reported as broadly equivalent with Euclidean, cosine, and correlation-based measures in Experiment 1. Alignment also varies across tasks and network layers; the best-aligned layer differs by model and experiment.

fits_no_version.finding: Model-to-human RDM alignment for quadrilaterals rises with training-set size (β=0.074, p=0.001); parameter count is not significant (p=0.26). The best models reach ~0.9 against a noise ceiling of 0.99.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Vision models' alignment with human geometric-shape perception scales mainly with training data size, not parameter count.

fits_no_version.finding: In Exp 2, alignment again tracks dataset size (β=0.024, p<1e-8), and the symbolic MDL adds unique predictive power (0.54 to 0.71 for Dinov3 small; 0.73 to 0.81 using all layers, ceiling 0.90).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Large vision models capture much but not all human geometric-shape difficulty; symbolic complexity adds unique variance.

fits_no_version.finding: In Exp 3, the best model (Dinov3 base) reaches rank 2.2 vs the human rank of 1. Training method was the top feature-importance predictor there.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Cross-format recognition of geometric drawings remains below human level; training method and data scale both matter.

fits_no_version.finding: Model rank-orders on human alignment correlate across the three tasks (r=0.46 to 0.67).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Human-alignment rankings of vision models are moderately consistent across geometric tasks.

fits_no_version.finding: Exp 1 results are equivalent with cosine and correlation distances, and Pearson and Spearman results are consistent.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Model-to-human geometric alignment is robust to the distance metric.

record.problems: The study measures alignment with group-average human behavior rather than model-to-model convergence. The authors note that parameter count and training dataset size are correlated (Pearson R = 0.32), and that dataset size may confound dataset composition and exposure to geometric stimuli. They also report relatively low reliability of individual judgments, preventing analysis of inter-individual variability. Experiment 3 uses 24 items, and no tested network reaches human-level performance there.
record.rows_left_out: No relevant reported outcomes were left out. Cited results from other studies were excluded.

untested.parts: No model-to-model representational alignment, so no test of whether it rises with scale; only model-to-human alignment vs dataset size.
No vision-language alignment on paired images and captions.
No comparison of seeds of the same architecture.
No mapping, stitching or relative-representation tests between models.
No matching of features or circuits across models.
Metric robustness checked only for model-to-human alignment, not model-to-model convergence.
Saturation of alignment (Exp 1) and the dataset-composition confound concern alignment with humans, not between models.

record.verdict_notes: The reader's T6/discusses call and its row links are correct. Any appeal to this paper as support for V1 would be indirect: convergence toward a shared human target implies, but does not measure, model-to-model convergence. The Exp 1 saturation remark (Discussion) bears on a V7-like plateau, but only for human alignment.

versions.untested_parts: No direct comparison of representational distances between independently trained models, or test of whether such model-to-model alignment increases with size or capability.
No measurement of vision-language representation alignment on paired images and captions as both models improve.
No comparison of networks trained from different initializations of the same architecture or test of shared features or subspaces.
No test of mapping one model's representations onto another's, stitching, relative representations, or alignment without paired data.
No test for recurring interpretable features or circuits across models.
Alternative distance metrics and task inputs are used to measure model-to-human alignment, not whether measured model-to-model convergence depends on metric settings or input distribution.
No direct test of whether model-to-model alignment is incomplete or plateaus, or whether shared training data or objectives explain such alignment.

relation.reason: The Discussion explicitly connects the findings to the Platonic representation hypothesis, but the study neither measures intermodel convergence nor uses it as a tool.

tranche.reason: The experiments measure model alignment with human geometric perception, not convergence between independently trained models or another listed claim version.

source_check.notes: Experiment 1's approximately 0.9 correlation remains below its 0.99 noise ceiling. In Experiment 3, training method has greater permutation importance than dataset size; model rank-order correlations across tasks do not measure intermodel representational alignment.
